title: If we confess (1 John 1:8–9)
hook: if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves

segments.voice: Yesterday, koinonia: the word of life, heard, seen and handled. Your line was seen and touched.

A map app can get you almost anywhere, on one condition: it has to know where you actually are. If the little blue dot thinks you're downtown when you're stuck on a country road, every direction it gives you will be wrong too, no matter how confident the voice sounds. It can't route you home from a place you're pretending to be. A few lines into his first letter, John says something very like this about the soul. And he says it to believers, not to strangers.
screen: `THE BLUE DOT HAS TO BE RIGHT.` → `NO ROUTE FROM A PRETEND PLACE.` → `JOHN SAYS IT TO BELIEVERS.`

segments.voice: The Douay-Rheims: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us." Notice the we. John doesn't point at outsiders; he includes himself, the one who touched the word of life. The danger isn't sin so much as pretending, putting the blue dot somewhere it isn't. Then the turn: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all iniquity." The Greek word for confess is homologeo, and some readers hear two pieces in it, same and say: to confess is to say the same thing, to agree with God about what actually happened. Not to grovel, not to perform, just to stop arguing with the truth. Then John picks two surprising words for God. Faithful, because God promised to forgive and keeps his promises. And just. You might expect justice to stand in the way of forgiveness. John puts it on forgiveness's side. A few verses later he explains: we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, who is the atonement for our sins. Catholics hear this passage in several places. Near the start of Mass, in what's called the penitential act, the people confess together that they have sinned, before they hear the word. And in the sacrament of Penance, a person names their sins to a priest and hears the words of absolution. The Catechism quotes these very verses when it says that to receive God's mercy, we have to admit our faults. Mercy can't reach a place you insist you aren't standing.
screen: `WE DECEIVE OURSELVES.` · `HOMOLOGEO: TO SAY THE SAME THING.` · `FAITHFUL AND JUST TO FORGIVE.` · `AT MASS AND IN CONFESSION.` · then, large: `IF WE CONFESS OUR SINS, HE IS FAITHFUL.`

segments.voice: Look back over the past few days and let one thing surface on its own: something you said, something you didn't do, a way you treated someone. Don't defend it and don't drown in it; say it plainly, in one sentence, the way it happened. If you pray, tell it to God and rest in John's line, he is faithful and just, to forgive; if not, let the plain naming be enough.
Homologeo, to confess. First John one: to say the same thing as the truth, and find God faithful and just to forgive. Today's word.
Your line: he is faithful to forgive. Faithful, and just. That's day six hundred fourteen.

screen: `DAY 614 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IN DEED AND IN TRUTH.`

howItsDone: Catholics confess their sins together in the penitential act near the start of Mass, and individually in the sacrament of Penance, where a person names their sins to a priest and receives absolution; the Church asks Catholics to confess serious sins at least once a year.

original.note: Greek: (if) we confess (1 John 1:9), often unpacked as homos, same, and legō, to say.

trapdoor: what you thought: confession means feeling terrible about yourself.
what it means: to agree with God about what really happened, and find him faithful and just to forgive.
what a scholar hears: homologeo, which readers unpack as 'to say the same thing'; and John calls God 'just' to forgive, setting justice on mercy's side because of Christ the advocate (1 John 2:1–2).

chat.says: If God already knows everything I did, why bother confessing it?
options: Confessing means agreeing with the truth, and God is faithful and just to forgive.
Because God only learns about a sin once you say it out loud to him.
Because confessing earns God's forgiveness, like paying off a debt.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): softened the homologeo etymology to what some readers hear; replaced 'almost every Mass' with the penitential act near the start of Mass; swapped the etymology myth for one on 'faithful and just'.
Homologeō from homos + legō ('say the same thing'): standard etymology. Confirm.
1 John 2:2: Douay-Rheims reads 'propitiation'; the script paraphrases with 'atonement'. Confirm the word choice.
CCC 1847 quotes 1 John 1:8–9 after 'To receive his mercy, we must admit our faults.' Paraphrased. Confirm.
Penitential act at the start of Mass ('almost every Mass': it can be replaced by the sprinkling rite or omitted in some combined rites). Confirm phrasing.
Annual confession of grave sins (CCC 1457). Confirm.
